turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, Mr Hale. The slip from the desk just says back, so start wherever you like. Is this your wife with you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sandra. I booked him in, or he'd still be at work pretending he's fine.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Back.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Low back, or higher?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Low.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left, right, or both?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Left.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long now?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Three.
[SEG0010] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's rounding it down. We moved house eight weeks ago, and it started that weekend, shifting wardrobes and boxes.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): What sort of work is it you do?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Warehouse.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heavy lifting in the warehouse, and that flares the pain?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Score it out of ten.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): Seven.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Constant, or on and off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Constant.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything take the edge off?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Lying.
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sofa every night. The dog's furious about the missed walks, and that animal thinks it runs the house.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dog out of the notes.
[SEG0023] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll be glad someone said it. Right, back to the back.

[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say the pain back to you. Left-sided low back pain, constant, seven out of ten, worse with lifting, eased by lying down. On timing you said three weeks and Sandra said eight, since the move, so I'll call it approximately three to eight weeks, not a precise date.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it travel into a leg?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): Leg.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): The leg pain, which leg, and how far down does it go?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Left calf.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Painkillers. What have you actually taken?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength are the tablets?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): Two hundred.
[SEG0034] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He buys four hundred milligram ibuprofen and takes two of them when it's bad.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): So for the ibuprofen I can't tell whether a dose is two hundred or eight hundred milligrams. I won't record a dose.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you taking them three times a day, as the packet usually says?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He isn't taking them three times a day. He forgets, then he has a handful at bedtime.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): So whether he takes them as directed is anyone's guess. Any other regular medicines?
[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Blood pressure.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you know its name?
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): White one.
[SEG0043] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Little white blood pressure tablet, every morning, for years. I almost called it amlodipine and that's me guessing, so scrub that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Unnamed blood pressure tablet it is. You've got high blood pressure, yes?
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or tingling in the legs or feet?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Problems with the waterworks at all?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Parking.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the car park. Passing urine. Hesitancy, leaking, anything like that?
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight down without trying?
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are your clothes looser?
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll treat that as not a proper yes. No weight loss recorded. Fevers, or drenching sweats?
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowel accidents, or numbness around the saddle, the groin and back passage?
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies?
[SEG0061] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the couch, please. Looking at you, lumbar flexion is limited, and you're tender in the left lower lumbar muscles.

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise on the left reproduces the calf pain at about fifty degrees. Power at the ankle and big toe is normal, no foot drop, and light touch on the foot is intact.

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking mechanical low back pain, nothing alarming in the answers so far. Plan A, then: no scan, stay on the ibuprofen, I refer you to physio now, and I see you in six weeks.
[SEG0065] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hang on. The toes. Tell the doctor what the van does.
[SEG0066] person_3 (PATIENT): Tingle.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): You said no numbness a minute ago. Which toes, and is it tingling?
[SEG0068] person_3 (PATIENT): Left. Sometimes.
[SEG0069] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left toes go tingly in the van. And the pain wakes him most nights. He's been up at two again.
[SEG0070] person_3 (PATIENT): Wakes.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): That new bit changes my mind. Scrap the immediate physio and the six-week review. The toe symptoms push this past a simple strain.

[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the ibuprofen. Start paracetamol, one gram by mouth, four times a day, for the back pain. I did wonder about naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day and I'm not doing that, not with the blood pressure tablet and an anti-inflammatory already.

[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange an MRI of the lumbar spine because of the left calf pain and the tingling toes. My working impression is mechanical low back pain with possible left nerve root irritation. A disc prolapse is on the differential, not a diagnosis I'll stamp today.

[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the scan is clear, we might refer you to physio afterwards. Keep moving gently, no heavy warehouse lifting until the scan is back, and if you cannot pass urine, develop saddle numbness, or a leg gives way, go to A&E the same day.
[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks.
[SEG0076] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We will.
[SEG0077] person_3 (PATIENT): Ta.

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient said the back pain had lasted three weeks while his wife said it began eight weeks ago at the house move, and the doctor summarised this as approximately three to eight weeks.
The patient said the ibuprofen strength was 200 mg but his wife said he takes two 400 mg tablets, so no single dose was recorded.
The patient said 'mm, I suppose' when asked if he takes ibuprofen three times a day, but his wife said he forgets doses and then takes a handful at night.
The regular morning blood pressure tablet could only be described as a little white tablet, and a guessed name was withdrawn.

Ibuprofen dose differs between the patient (200 mg) and his wife (two 400 mg tablets).
ambiguous_entities: Ibuprofen three-times-daily use was answered with 'mm, I suppose', which was not taken as a clear yes.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
